High-school physics teaches us that human hearing spans 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. At university, once we learn the sampling theorem, we find that the minimum sampling rate for audio only needs to be twice the upper limit of hearing, which is 40 kHz. Yet most of the audio we encounter is sampled at 44.1 kHz. This article looks at why. You could call it convention, but like most conventions, it owes something to historical accident.

1. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem

The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem states that to convert a continuous signal, such as an audio waveform, accurately into digital form, the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal. This is the fundamental requirement for reconstructing the signal correctly.

  • Range of human hearing: human hearing is generally taken to span 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).

  • To capture frequencies up to 20 kHz without aliasing (distortion), the sampling rate must be at least 40 kHz.

  • 44.1 kHz was therefore chosen as the standard: it sits slightly above twice 20 kHz and so captures every frequency in the range of human hearing.

But that raises the question: why 44.1 kHz and not 40 kHz?


2. Compatibility with early video equipment

The choice of 44.1 kHz is closely tied to compatibility with early video equipment:

  • It goes back to the PCM adaptors of the late 1970s, which were used to record digital audio onto videotape.

  • Television had by then moved from black and white to color, and there were two main broadcast standards, PAL and NTSC. The sample rates they yield are shown below:

  • The PCM adaptor’s sampling rate had to fit the existing video formats, which made it easy to store audio alongside the large body of television video material that already existed. The PCM adaptor in turn laid the foundation for the later CD (Compact Disc) standard.

3. Establishing a consumer audio standard

Once 44.1 kHz was settled as the standard sampling rate, it spread quickly through consumer audio. CD players, home stereo systems, recording software and other equipment were all designed around it.

  • Compatibility: because 44.1 kHz became the standard, almost all audio hardware and software supports it, which made it the industry standard for consumer audio worldwide.

  • Ubiquity: 44.1 kHz is widely used in CDs, MP3s and other formats, which further cemented its status as the standard for digital audio.

4. CD storage capacity

A CD holds 700 MB, so storing audio on it means balancing sound quality against file size. A sampling rate of 44.1 kHz combined with a 16-bit depth (the number of bits per sample) makes efficient use of the disc while delivering good enough sound quality.

  • With 44.1 kHz, 16 bits and stereo (two channels), each CD can hold roughly 74–80 minutes of audio at good quality, enough for most albums.

5. The trade-off between quality and storage

A sampling rate of 44.1 kHz offers good sound quality and efficient use of storage:

  • Sound quality: 44.1 kHz captures content above the range of human hearing, which ensures high-fidelity sound.

  • File size and storage: higher sampling rates (such as 96 kHz or 192 kHz) produce larger files, which ordinary music playback usually does not need, especially since 44.1 kHz already sounds good enough.

Are there alternatives?

  • 48 kHz: the standard for video production and professional audio, because it offers a slightly better frequency response than 44.1 kHz (capturing frequencies up to 24 kHz). It is less common in consumer audio formats, although it is widely used on DVD, Blu-ray and in video recording.

  • Higher sampling rates (such as 96 kHz and 192 kHz): these are mostly used in high-resolution audio formats, professional recording and studio work, where finer detail, more headroom or a better frequency response may be needed. For the typical music listener, though, the difference is usually imperceptible.

The metaverse, virtual reality and spatial audio may have lost some of their buzz, but they are still where things are heading. So here’s the question: do you think 44.1 kHz will eventually be replaced?

Share your thoughts in the comments: type 1 if you think it will, 2 if you think it won’t!
